title: Stage 2: Modelling an expense
summary: Give the data a shape: a record, an enum, real dates, and decimal for money.

steps.title: From strings to an Expense
body: Stage 1 left you with rows of strings. Strings are a poor way to hold data: you cannot add `"45.50"` to `"12.00"`, and nothing stops `"Travle"` from being a category.
In this stage you give the data a **shape**. Each row becomes an `Expense` with a real date, a category from a fixed list, and an amount you can do arithmetic on. For this input:
the program will print every expense in one tidy format, and by the end of the stage a total:
Notice `45.5` and `12` came out as `45.50` and `12.00`. That only happens once they are numbers.
For now, assume every line is well formed. Stage 3 deals with the ones that are not.

steps.prompt: Each column deserves its own type. Drag each value to the type that should hold it.
steps.explain: A date with no time of day is a `DateOnly`. The category is one of a small fixed set, which is what an enum is for. Money is a `decimal`. Only the description is free text.

steps.title: A record, an enum, and three parsers
body: The domain fits in two lines. They go at the **bottom** of the file, after all the statements:
enum Category { Travel, Meals, Lodging, Supplies, Other }
record Expense(DateOnly Date, Category Category, decimal Amount, string Description);
Each column has its own way from text to value:
- `ParseExact` takes the **format** you expect: four-digit year, two-digit month, two-digit day. `MM` is month; lowercase `mm` would mean minutes.

- `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` says *this is data, not something typed by a local user*. In Germany `45,50` is how people write forty-five and a half. A data file must mean the same thing on every machine, so you name the culture instead of trusting the computer's settings.
`CultureInfo` lives in a namespace that is not imported for you. Put this on the **first line** of the file:

steps.prompt: Match each column value to the code that turns it into the right type.
pairs: nothing: it is already the right type

steps.prompt: `amount` is the `decimal` value `45.5m`. Which line prints `45.50`?
steps.explain: After a colon comes a **format**. `F2` means fixed-point with two decimal places. With no format you get `45.5`. A comma sets a minimum width, not the number of decimals.

steps.title: Parse each expense
prompt: 1. At the bottom of the file add the `Category` enum (`Travel`, `Meals`, `Lodging`, `Supplies`, `Other`) and the record `Expense(DateOnly Date, Category Category, decimal Amount, string Description)`.
2. Write a method `Expense ParseExpense(string line)` that splits one line and parses each column.
3. Replace the list of rows with a `List<Expense>`.

4. Write a method `string Describe(Expense expense)` that returns one expense as `date | category | amount | description`, with the date as `yyyy-MM-dd` and the amount with two decimal places. Print every expense with it.
5. Change the last line to say `Expenses:` instead of `Rows:`.
Keep skipping blank lines and the header. For this input:
Every line in this stage is well formed, so `Parse` is fine for now.
solution: return new Expense(date, category, amount, parts[3]);
enum Category { Travel, Meals, Lodging, Supplies, Other }
record Expense(DateOnly Date, Category Category, decimal Amount, string Description);

require.message: Stores the date as a DateOnly

hints: Top of the file: `using System.Globalization;`. In the loop: `expenses.Add(ParseExpense(line));`.
Inside `ParseExpense`: `var parts = line.Split(',');` then parse `parts[0]`, `parts[1]` and `parts[2]` as on the card, and `return new Expense(date, category, amount, parts[3]);`.

steps.title: Why money is a decimal
body: `double` stores numbers in binary. Most decimal fractions, including `0.1`, have no exact binary form, so a `double` holds the nearest value it can. The error is tiny, but it is there, and it grows as you add.
For a physics simulation that is fine. For money it is a bug: totals that are a cent out, and two amounts that should be equal but are not.
`decimal` stores numbers in base ten, the way you write them. `0.1m` is exactly one tenth.
The rule in real codebases is short: **money is `decimal`, always**. The `m` suffix on a literal stands for *money*.

steps.prompt: Same sum, two types. What does this print?
steps.explain: The `double` sum is `0.30000000000000004`, which is not the `double` nearest to `0.3`. The `decimal` sum is exactly `0.3`.

prompt: A list of expenses wants a total. Because `Amount` is a `decimal`, adding them up is exact.
After the `Expenses:` line, print the sum of all amounts with two decimal places:
